name: Liberal feminism
scope: Liberal feminism as its defining sources describe it: the branch of feminism that seeks women's equality through political and legal reform within liberal democracy, centred on women's personal and political autonomy, equal civil and political rights, and equal access to education, employment and public life (s1, s2, s3). It runs from Wollstonecraft and John Stuart Mill (s2, s4) through Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (s4) to the egalitarian-liberal philosophy of Okin and Nussbaum, who extend Rawls to women's concerns (s2, s3). The Stanford Encyclopedia separates an egalitarian-liberal strand from a classical-liberal (equity, libertarian) strand (s2); both count as liberal feminism, and the answers record where they split. It is set against socialist, Marxist and radical feminism (s1, s3), which are other ideologies and do not answer.

summary: Liberal feminism seeks women's equality through legal and political reform inside liberal democracy: equal political and civil rights (Wollstonecraft, Mill), equal education and opportunity (Friedan), and, in the egalitarian-liberal strand, anti-discrimination law, access to birth control and abortion, and equal recognition of family forms. Classical-liberal strands favour limited state action. Its sources state few positions beyond these, so most statements stay unanswered.
